catalog_quote: [p. 64] In Dolakha Newar, when words are pronounced in isolation, the first syllable is the most prominent, so can be said to be stressed. The primary cue for stress is pitch, which correlates with the acoustic property of fundamental frequency. On disyllabic words pronounced in isolation, there is a slight rise in pitch in the first syllable and then a fall through the rest of the word. Intensity, another feature commonly found to mark stress, plays a relatively marginal role in this language ... Length does not seem to be relevant to stress ... Disyllabic words formed by the addition of a verbal prefix follow the same pattern as disyllabic monomorphemic words. ... In words of three syllables pronounced in isolation, stress decreases with each successive syllable, such that the third syllable is lowest in fundamental frequency and intensity. new_statements.quote: [p.64] In Dolakha Newar, when words are pronounced in isolation, the first syllable is the most prominent, so can be said to be stressed. The primary cue for stress is pitch ... Length does not seem to be relevant to stress ... [p.68] It is possible to analyze the prominence on the initial syllable as resulting from an intonation pattern specific to words in isolation. At this point, there does not appear to be strong support of either analysis. What is clear is that if one analyzes Dolakha Newar as having first-syllable stress, it clearly has a very low functional load. It is predictable, not phonemic, and is largely obscured by intonation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word in citation forms, including on a verbal prefix when one is present (mwa-mwal patterns like a monomorphemic disyllable; p. 44: stress is on the 'phonetically initial syllable'); it is predictable and non-contrastive, cued mainly by an F0 peak on syllable 1 with steady fall thereafter, and the author explicitly hedges that the pattern might instead be an isolation-form intonation contour. Genetti 2003: 357 states it more flatly: 'Dolakhae has stress but no tone. Stress falls on the initial syllable of a root'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Genetti 2003: 357: 'with a secondary stress on third syllables in longer words.' Genetti 2007: 64 instead reports that in trisyllables pronounced in isolation prominence (F0 and intensity) decreases with each successive syllable; no secondary-stress rule is stated in the 2007 grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: None lexical. Clitics/particles and several bound morphemes are described as not independently stressed (e.g. pp. ~97-105, 250ff.); Nepali loans not singled out for stress. The only caveat is analytic: stress vs. isolation intonation undecided, 'very low functional load'.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly citation/isolation forms of the phonological word (root plus prefixes, suffixes and enclitics; first-syllable stress is listed as criterion (3) for phonological wordhood). In connected speech 'the word-level stress pattern is often obscured by the phrasal intonation contours' and 'lexical stress is thus subordinated to phrasal intonation' (pp. 66-67). No tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Dolakha Newar (Dolakhae), the variety spoken in Dolakha village ~145 km east of Kathmandu; Glottolog 5.1 treats Dolakha Newar as the reference variety of the language-level languoid east2773 'Eastern Newari' (no separate dialect glottocode; ISO [new] is shared with Kathmandu Valley Newari newa1246). Statement should be catalogued as Dolakha Newar = east2773, not as Kathmandu Newar.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the newly opened works and the catalog: Genetti & Slater 2004 describes only phrase-level prosodic accent and Genetti 1986 (Kathmandu-type 'Newari') says nothing about stress, so the catalog's fixed: initial syllable reading (Genetti 2007: 64, 68; Genetti 2003: 357 'Stress falls on the initial syllable of a root, with a secondary stress on third syllables in longer words') stands. One caveat worth recording, found while cross-checking the phrasal-accent references: Genetti 2007: 72 (Ch. 3 sec. 3, already held by the project) says that in polysyllabic words bearing phrasal accent 'the accent [may be] realized on any syllable of the word. In words with initial aspirated consonants or affricates, the initial syllable is likely to be the most prominent. Otherwise, the acoustic prominence delivered by phrasal accent appears most commonly to be on the final syllable of the word. Further investigation into this issue is warranted.' Genetti 2011 (Himalayan Linguistics 10(1), fn. 10, downloaded incidentally) defers to that passage. This is a phrase-level realization statement, not a word-stress statement, and Genetti 2007: 64-68 explicitly leaves open whether the isolation-form initial prominence is lexical stress or an intonation pattern; so the catalog entry is best understood as 'initial prominence in isolation forms; phrasal accent may fall elsewhere in connected speech'.
